title: We Keep Telling Kids to Go Outside and Play. Then We Give Them Nowhere Worthwhile to Go.
author: Kevin Stinehart
summary: Stinehart argues that the standard advice to send kids outside fails not because children resist it but because the physical and social infrastructure that once made spontaneous play possible - reachable friends, open schoolyards, unscheduled time, safe streets - has been dismantled, turning free play into a collective-action problem no single family can solve alone. He distinguishes "outputs" like collaboration, self-regulation, and resilience, which adults now try to teach directly, from the system of unstructured play that actually produces them, arguing worksheets and SEL lessons can describe these capacities but not generate them. Drawing on his own school's Play Club and a pilot "Playbrary" project in Central, South Carolina, he reframes the fix as removing barriers - unlocking playgrounds, slowing traffic, stocking flexible loose-play materials - rather than adding more adult-run enrichment programming. The piece closes by treating towns as already designing childhood by default, through zoning, recreation-department policy, and school playground access, whether or not they intend to.
points: Restoring play is reframed as a collective-action problem: one family opting out of screens can't recreate a neighborhood of available playmates, safe routes, or open schoolyards on its own.
Capacities like self-regulation, resilience, and negotiation are 'system outputs' of unstructured play, not skills a lesson can install - a worksheet can describe the process but can't reproduce it.
Schools that protect recess and movement still can't rebuild a play-filled evening or neighborhood - the fix requires towns, planners, and civic institutions, not just teachers.

His concrete intervention, a 90-day 'Playbrary' pilot stocking a public field with free, no-registration play materials, tests whether removing friction is enough to generate spontaneous play, rather than adding more programming.
Screens win by default because they have almost no friction; the practical argument is that communities must make the physical world easier to enter, not just lecture kids away from devices.
quotes: The hardest part of getting children off screens is not convincing them to go outside. It is giving them an outside world worth entering.

One family cannot manufacture a neighborhood full of children outside ready and waiting to play. It cannot build sidewalks, slow traffic, unlock a schoolyard, or make five other families protect the same unscheduled afternoon.

Adults increasingly describe collaboration, self-regulation, resilience, conflict resolution, and independence as skills children must be taught. They can be named, modeled, and supported, but they cannot be installed through a lesson. They are system outputs.
A worksheet or an SEL lesson can describe that process. It cannot reproduce it.
Communities build infrastructure around what they care about. Libraries lower the friction of reading. Walking paths lower the friction of walking. Parks should lower the friction of play.

Screens win partly because they have almost no friction. Friends and entertainment are instantly available - no ride, equipment, coordination, or wandering is required. We will not lecture children out of an environment designed this way.
The answer is not another adult-run enrichment hour called “Unstructured Play.” Children do not need a Director of Spontaneous Fun standing in the park with a clipboard.
